title: Here Are the First Images of the Crater Left on the Moon by SpaceX’s Rocket
gist: South Korea's Danuri lunar orbiter, operated by the Korea Aerospace Research Institute, captured the first before-and-after images of the crater left when a SpaceX Falcon 9 second stage struck the moon after more than a year in an unstable orbit. SpaceX conceded that controlled deorbiting is not always possible on high-energy lunar-transfer missions and says it is collaborating with NASA on disposal solutions.

insights.claim: South Korea's Danuri orbiter, flying at 62 miles (100 kilometers) altitude, produced the first before-and-after imagery of the Falcon 9 impact site, beating NASA's own lunar orbiters to publication.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Korea demonstrating first-mover lunar observation capability is a credible entry signal for KARI and Korean space contractors into cislunar services.
insights.locator: The Korea Aerospace Research Institute shared the first photographs

insights.claim: Only a small number of nations currently operate satellites in lunar orbit, making orbital imaging of the moon's surface a scarce and strategically held capability.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Scarcity of lunar orbital assets means cislunar situational awareness is a contested capability gap — a procurement theme for space primes.
insights.quote: South Korea is one of the few nations that currently has satellites traveling around the moon
insights.locator: The Korea Aerospace Research Institute shared

insights.claim: NASA warned days before the collision that observing the impact moment would be difficult due to weather and timing, despite astronomers having predicted the time and place well in advance.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Prediction is far ahead of observation capacity in cislunar space — a gap that space-domain-awareness vendors are positioned to fill.
insights.locator: Astronomers predicted when and where the Falcon 9 impact would happen

insights.claim: Astronomers projected the impact would create a crater dozens of feet wide and nearly 12 feet (3.6 meters) deep, and the released imagery shows a crater larger than several cars combined.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Quantified debris-impact damage gives regulators a concrete basis for cislunar disposal rules currently governed only by voluntary practice.
insights.locator: The images show signs of a recent impact

insights.claim: The Very Large Telescope detected sodium and lithium rising from the lunar surface after the event, spectroscopically confirming that the rocket fragment struck the moon.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Ground-based spectroscopy can independently verify cislunar impacts, meaning attribution of space-debris events no longer depends on the operator's own telemetry.
insights.quote: astronomers detected sodium and lithium rising from the lunar surface, confirming that the rocket fragment did indeed strike the moon
insights.locator: This evidence of the collision adds to observations

insights.claim: SpaceX stated that on high-energy missions to lunar transfer orbit nearly all vehicle performance goes to placing the payload, so a controlled deorbiting maneuver is not always possible — an explicit admission that its standard ocean-reentry disposal does not extend to deep-space missions.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: A structural performance-versus-disposal trade-off means abandoned upper stages will keep accumulating as lunar launch cadence rises — regulatory exposure for launch providers.
insights.quote: nearly all of the vehicle’s performance is dedicated to successfully placing the payload into the intended orbit, and a controlled deorbiting maneuver is not always possible

insights.claim: The Falcon 9 stage launched in January 2025 and spent more than a year in an unstable orbit while Earth, moon, and solar gravity plus solar activity progressively deflected its trajectory until it hit the moon.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Multi-body perturbation makes abandoned cislunar hardware effectively untrackable over year-long horizons, raising the cost of any future custody or liability regime.

insights.claim: SpaceX says it is collaborating with NASA to find an optimal disposal solution for hardware left in higher-energy orbits, signaling that cislunar debris disposal is an unsolved operational problem rather than a settled procedure.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: An acknowledged gap between agency and prime contractor is where new disposal-services and tracking contracts get created.
insights.quote: we are collaborating with NASA to find the optimal disposal solution
